title: The House That Grew on the Cliff: Decoding Hongya Cave
summary: Six fifth-grade students investigated how Hongya Cave’s stilt houses stand on a vertical cliff face. Through field observation, historical research at the Three Gorges Museum, and physical modeling, they discovered that the building is not just constructed but 'grown' from the mountain using diagonal bracing and flood-adaptive design.

timeline.d: Before leaving for Chongqing, the team attempted to build cardboard models of stilt houses in the classroom.

moments.d: Their first attempt failed dramatically when the model collapsed at the third layer.
By adding diagonal supports (bracing), they successfully stabilized the second prototype, learning the physics before seeing the real thing.

timeline.d: Upon arriving in Chongqing, students went directly to the riverside below Hongya Cave to inspect the structural base.

moments.d: Ignoring the tourist crowds above, the group crouched near the water to measure platform widths with tape measures.
They observed that pillars on the river side were significantly longer than those on the mountain side, relying on stone platforms for footing.

timeline.d: The journey moved indoors to understand the context of the city's topography and history.

moments.d: At the China Three Gorges Museum, photos revealed that old Chongqing was once densely packed with these specific types of riverside structures.
From Qiansimen Bridge, students sketched cross-sections confirming the building stacks vertically from Binjiang Road up to Cangbai Road.

timeline.d: A crucial insight came from interviewing a local vendor about the function of the lowest floors.

moments.d: Students noticed discoloration on lower pillars; a local auntie explained this was the high-water mark during floods.
They realized the bottom floor is intentionally left empty or used for movable goods so it can 'yield' to nature without destroying the home.

timeline.d: Back at the hotel, the team synthesized their sketches, interviews, and measurements into final outputs.

moments.d: Using straws and paperboard, they rebuilt their initial concept, proving that diagonal bracing makes the structure rigid against shaking.
The group presented their findings to younger students, explaining that buildings can grow along slopes rather than sitting flat on land.

storyline.theme: How Chongqing's architecture adapts to steep terrain and rising waters.

storyline.question: Why can Hongya Cave's stilt houses be built on such a steep cliff?
subQuestions: Why don't the wooden pillars inserted into the cliff cause the house to fall over?
Why does every floor of an eleven-story building feel like the ground level when you walk out?
Why did people living by the river historically build their homes this way?

openQuestions.q: Are there other old houses in Chongqing still 'growing' on slopes today?
openQuestions.d: To see if this architectural style survives outside of famous landmarks.

openQuestions.q: If we build on an even steeper slope, how many more pillars are needed?
openQuestions.d: Testing the limits of the structural engineering principles they learned.

openQuestions.q: Can traditional wood withstand modern tourism loads?
openQuestions.d: Investigating the durability of heritage sites under heavy foot traffic.

outcomes: Produced a 12-page illustrated report titled 'Why Stilt Houses Can Stand on Cliffs'.
Created functional straw-and-cardboard models demonstrating diagonal bracing stability.
Completed 9 detailed site sketches capturing column bases and eaves.
Delivered a school-wide presentation on adaptive mountain architecture.
